words_and_claims_to_avoid: Government look-alike design, 'official notice', fake checks or invoices (39 USC 3001)
Unsubstantiated 'best', '#1', 'voted #1', 'guaranteed results', percent-savings claims (FTC Act s.5)
Invented or composite testimonials, star ratings or review counts (16 CFR 255)
'Free' unless it truly costs nothing and carries no hidden obligation (16 CFR 251)
Fake expiration dates or fake scarcity; any deadline printed must be real
Demographic/age targeting language (e.g., 'seniors', 'retirees') unless the client has evidence it fits their actual buyers
Any vendor case-study result (calls, ROI, revenue) printed as if it were the client's own result
'Safe', 'harmless', 'non-toxic', 'nonpoisonous', 'pet-safe', 'kid-safe', 'family-safe', 'safe for the environment' (federal + state pesticide rules)
'Pest-free guaranteed', 'kills 100%', 'eliminates all' without substantiation and a real guarantee
'Pet-friendly' or 'kid-friendly' lawn treatments (reads as a safety claim; banned in several states)
'Adds X% to your home value' unless quoting NAR's exact estimate, source and year
'Interest-free' or '0% for 24 months' without full Reg Z disclosures
compliance_notes: If the sale closes in the home: FTC Cooling-Off Rule (16 CFR 429) applies to $25+ in-home sales; the client's contract must carry the 3-day cancel notice. States can add longer windows.

Print the client's contractor license number where the state requires it in ads; requirements vary by state, and the client must confirm their own state's rule (we only verified the specific state rules named below).
Any discount or 'save X%' must be off a real, recently charged price; 'save 40%' with no reference price is not allowed.

Reg Z, 12 CFR 1026.24 (verified): if a card states a down payment amount or %, the number of payments or repayment period (e.g., 'for 24 months', 'no payments for 12 months'), a payment amount ('$99/mo'), or a finance charge amount, it must also state the down payment, the full repayment terms and the 'annual percentage rate' using that term. Any rate (e.g., '0%') must be stated as an APR. Terms must be ones actually offered. Safe alternative: 'Financing available', which uses no trigger terms. Have the lender review.

FTC 'Free' Guide, 16 CFR 251 (verified): (1) 'free with purchase' means the paid item is at its regular price (sold openly for about 30 days), with no markup or downgrade to cover the free item; (2) all conditions go right next to the offer, not in an asterisk footnote; (3) if the main job is priced by negotiation or bid, 'free [item] with purchase' is improper; (4) don't run the same 'free' offer more than 6 months in any 12; (5) 'gift' or 'bonus' wording doesn't cure a deceptive 'free'.

Warranty ads, 16 CFR 239 + 702 (verified): 'lifetime/life' must say whose or what life (239.4); 'satisfaction/money-back guarantee' only if the full price is refunded on request, with conditions disclosed (239.3); advertise a warranty only if it is promptly honored (239.5); ads should say where the full warranty can be seen (239.2).
Testimonials and star ratings must be real, typical and current; disclose any material connection (16 CFR 255).

Lawn treatments that use pesticides (weed control, grub control, fertilizer-plus-herbicide) fall under pesticide ad rules: Pesticide safety claims (verified): never say 'safe', 'harmless', 'non-toxic', 'nonpoisonous', 'pet-safe', 'kid-safe', 'eco-safe', with or without 'when used as directed'. Federal label rule 40 CFR 156.10(a)(5)(ix)-(x); explicit ad bans in TX (4 TAC 7.152), NJ (N.J.A.C. 7:30-2.12), CA (16 CCR 1999.5) and CO (C.R.S. 35-9-120). Assume every state is at least this strict until the client confirms.
No 'EPA approved', 'EPA registered' or anything implying government endorsement (40 CFR 156.10(a)(5)(v); TX 7.152(a)(5); CA 1999.5).
'Organic', 'natural', 'green', 'environmentally friendly' for pesticide services are banned outright in TX and NJ and need narrow substantiation elsewhere (FTC Green Guides 16 CFR 260).

Texas (verified): 4 TAC 7.152 applies to structural pest control licensees, and the Texas SPCS program has Lawn & Ornamental and Weed Control categories (4 TAC 7.124). Some for-hire lawn applicators instead hold an agricultural applicator license (3A/5), so the client must confirm which rules apply; the safety-claim ban is the safe default either way.
California landscape contractors (C-27) fall under B&P 7030.5: license number in all advertising (verified for contractors generally).
Recurring programs: state the price, frequency and how to cancel next to the offer; a 'free first treatment with program' must be at the program's regular price (16 CFR 251).
standing_rules: Emotion-agnostic: fear, disgust, joy, pride, status, relief are all options; the client chooses.
Every angle and combo carries a sell-the-outcome line.
Unverified (agency/vendor-only) results are labeled; never quote them as fact on a card.

emotion_by_offer_conflicts.conflict: GOLD-landscaping-005 'IT'S INTEREST-FREE!' + '0% APR for 24 months' vs Reg Z
emotion_by_offer_conflicts.resolution: Compliance wins: '24 months' triggers full disclosure. Keep the outcome headline; put financing as a support line with full terms, or 'Financing available'.

emotion_by_offer_conflicts.conflict: GOLD-landscaping-002 reports 6,563% ROI (PostcardMania) vs never print unverified results
emotion_by_offer_conflicts.resolution: Vendor-published, unaudited; use only as weak evidence that free-design offers can pull.

emotion_by_offer_conflicts.conflict: Lawn Doctor 'Don't be embarrassed' (shame) vs 'positive pride' angles
emotion_by_offer_conflicts.resolution: Both allowed (emotion-agnostic). Client chooses; offer both versions.

emotion_by_offer_conflicts.conflict: Lawn treatment marketing commonly says 'pet-safe' vs pesticide ad rules
emotion_by_offer_conflicts.resolution: Law wins: no safety claims for pesticide treatments. If a product is not a pesticide (e.g., plain fertilizer), the client must still substantiate any safety claim under FTC Act s.5.
